extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media critics, and informed readers interested in press ethics and newsroom decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Judgment framework for whether and how a news outlet should publish leaked/unverified intelligence documents (e.g., the Steele dossier), including legal defenses, ethical considerations, and editorial practices such as caveats and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing unverified information (gold standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not publishing unverified information—particularly when it's been commissioned by political operatives—remains a gold standard in many quarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece frames initial media reluctance to publish unverified material as understandable given public trust concerns. Editors should default to verification where possible, and treat commission by political actors as a heightened reason for caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominently caveat publication of unverified documents
rubrics_metrics.description: BuzzFeed prominently caveated its release of the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a newsroom decides to publish material that is not fully verified, it should include clear, prominent caveats and contextual explanations so readers understand the provenance and limits of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / right to know as justification
rubrics_metrics.description: A document that had been circulating at the highest levels of government, under active investigation by the FBI, and briefed to two successive presidents ... is clearly the subject of 'official action.' Publication has contributed to the American people’s understanding of what is happening in their country and their government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should weigh whether a leaked document is connected to government action or investigation and whether publication materially serves the public’s understanding; such connections strengthen the public-interest case for release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal privilege when document is involved in government proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal judge ... dismissed the claim ... on First Amendment grounds, finding that publication was privileged because the dossier was involved in government proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should consider whether the material was part of government proceedings or official action, since that can create a stronger legal protection against defamation claims. Legal context can influence but does not solely determine editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducing documents without expressing an opinion can support legal defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge found BuzzFeed’s report was 'fair and true' because it reproduced the dossier without expressing an opinion on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing controversial documents, presenting them neutrally (quoting/reproducing rather than endorsing) may improve legal defensibility—though it is not an ethical panacea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal vindication is distinct from ethical vindication
rubrics_metrics.description: Winning a court case on First Amendment grounds is not the same thing as winning an ethical argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if publication is legally protected, editors should separately assess the ethical dimensions (harm, verification, motives) before claiming moral vindication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sensational specific allegations skeptically unless evidence supports them
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of its more sensational claims were likely false ... 'we have not seen the evidence to support them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the overall significance of a document (e.g., demonstration of foreign interference) and discrete sensational allegations within it; seek corroborating evidence for specific claims before presenting them as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full publication can move a story forward when existence already reported
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of the dossier had already been reported. By putting the whole thing online, BuzzFeed moved the story forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reporting has already established that a document exists, publishing the full text may help transparency and enable broader scrutiny; this is an editorial consideration that can justify publication even when specifics aren't fully verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider media environment and public trust when deciding
rubrics_metrics.description: The media’s hypersensitivity around facts was an understandable initial response to Trump’s victory, which served as a jarring reminder of threadbare public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should account for prevailing public trust, recent misinformation dynamics, and potential backlash when choosing whether and how to publish contested materials; what is defensible in one context may be reckless in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source/commissioning party affects credibility and requires extra scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly when it's been commissioned by political operatives ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material commissioned by partisan or political actors should be treated with heightened skepticism; newsrooms should disclose commissioning provenance and apply stricter verification and contextualization standards.
